ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a Darlington pair transistor circuit. On the left there is a DC power supply labeled 48 V, with its lower end grounded. The positive terminal of the power supply biases the base of the first transistor through a wire; next to the first transistor is labeled β = 90. The emitter of the first transistor is connected to the base of the second transistor, and next to the second transistor is labeled β = 25. The emitter of the second transistor is connected to a 100 Ω resistor, the lower end of the resistor is grounded, and the current is labeled I4. Reasoning: According to the problem statement, the forward base-emitter voltage drop of each transistor is taken as 0.7 V. The first emitter voltage is approximately 48 - 0.7 = 47.3 V. The second emitter voltage drops another 0.7 V, so it is 47.3 - 0.7 = 46.6 V. Therefore, the voltage across the 100 Ω resistor is approximately 46.6 V. By Ohm's law, I4 = 46.6 V / 100 Ω = 0.466 A = 466 mA.

raw_record.question_text: Calculate current I\(_4\) in this Darlington pair circuit, assuming a typical forward base-emitter junction voltage drop of 0.7 volts for each transistor. The current I\(_4\) is ______ mA.

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram: a 48 V source biases the base of the first transistor in a Darlington pair, two base-emitter junctions appear in series before the second emitter, and the second emitter is connected to a 100 ohm resistor to ground where I4 flows. Treat the first emitter as 48 - 0.7 = 47.3 V and the second emitter as 47.3 - 0.7 = 46.6 V. The 100 ohm resistor therefore has 46.6 V across it, so I4 = 46.6/100 = 0.466 A = 466 mA.
